passage:
Kaito, the regional manager in Osaka, closed the door and slid a one-page summary across the table. "I want to tell you myself why the senior planner role went to Rieko. Two things: she has run the vendor renegotiation twice, and she writes shorter handovers than any of us."

Sami read it twice. His first instinct was to argue that his numbers were better. He kept his pen still and asked, "Is the handover point fair?"

"It is. Your last two took nine pages, and people skipped them."

Sami nodded. It stung, but he could see it was true. "What would make you reconsider me next cycle?"

"Lead one vendor talk end to end, and cut the handovers to two pages. If you do both, I'll put your name forward."

Sami wrote both down. "Thank you for being straight with me."

"You've earned that," Kaito said.

qa.q: What two reasons did Kaito give for choosing Rieko?
qa.a: Kaito said Rieko had run the vendor renegotiation twice and wrote shorter handovers than anyone else.

qa.q: What did Sami feel at first, and how do we know?
qa.a: Sami's first instinct was to argue that his numbers were better, which shows defensiveness, but he kept his pen still and listened.

qa.q: What did Sami do that made the feedback useful?
qa.a: He accepted the fair point about long handovers and asked what would change the decision next cycle, turning feedback into two concrete steps.

qa.q: Why might Kaito have chosen to tell Sami in person?
qa.a: Kaito probably wanted to show respect by giving an honest reason rather than leaving Sami to guess, and by saying what could lead to a different result.

grounding: A boss honestly explains why someone else got the role; Sami takes the feedback without defensiveness and asks what would change next cycle.

passage:
Payal: Kunal, got a sec? Wanted to tell you myself before the email goes out.
Payal: The senior analyst role went to Ritu. I know you wanted it.
Kunal: Oh. Okay.
Payal: Honest reason: her client presentations are stronger. Yours are solid on numbers but you lose the room in the first five minutes.
Kunal: That's...fair, I think. It stings, but fair.
Payal: Your data work is the best on the team, that's not in question.
Kunal: What would I need to show to get it next time?
Payal: Present to clients three times before March. I'll put you on the Nagpur account. Ask Ritu for feedback too.
Kunal: Okay. Can we check in after each one?
Payal: Yes. And thanks for taking this so well.
Kunal: 😅 I'll go be sad for ten minutes, then I'm in.

qa.q: Who got the senior analyst role?
What does Kunal's reply "It stings, but fair" show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows he feels disappointed and hurt, but is willing to accept the honest reason without getting defensive.

qa.q: How did Kunal use the conversation to prepare for the next cycle?
qa.a: He asked what he would need to show next time, accepted the plan to present to clients before March, and asked for check-ins.

qa.q: How might Payal see Kunal's response?
qa.a: Payal may feel relieved and appreciative that her honest feedback was taken well, making her more willing to support him.

grounding: A boss explains honestly why someone else got the role; the protagonist takes it without defensiveness and asks what would change next cycle.

passage:
At the seed company's depot office in Barshi, Chaitanya sir called Neelam in after the monthly review. "I wanted to tell you face to face. The area supervisor post is going to Sunil."
Neelam's throat tightened. She had covered the rain-hit villages alone in August.
"Why him?" It came out sharper than she meant.
"Two reasons. He has kept the dealer accounts clean for a year without a single mismatch. Yours had three errors this season. And he has trained the new sales boys. Your field work is excellent, but you do it alone."
She wanted to argue about August. She stopped herself and nodded. "The accounts part is fair. The training, I never got the chance."
"Then take it. Train the two new ones in January. And we'll review your accounts monthly."
"If I do both, would it change things next time?"
"It would."

qa.q: How many errors did Neelam's dealer accounts have this season?
What was Neelam feeling when Chaitanya sir told her the post was going to Sunil?
qa.a: She felt hurt and disappointed, her throat tightening, since she had covered the rain-hit villages alone in August.

qa.q: How did Neelam handle the feedback well?
qa.a: She stopped herself from arguing, agreed the accounts point was fair, and asked what would change the decision next time.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya sir see the conversation?
qa.a: He likely feels respected and relieved that Neelam listened, and willing to give her the training chance.

grounding: A boss explains honestly why someone else got the role; the protagonist notes what is fair and asks what would change the decision next cycle.
